resident.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old female presented with a nine-month decline in lower extremity strength and ambulation ability.
resident.history: This 44-year-old female presented with a decline in lower extremity strength and ambulation ability over nine months. She also reported increased numbness of the lower extremities, worsening lower back pain, bowel incontinence, neck pain, and paresthesias, numbness, and weakness of the upper extremities. The record contains no separate laboratory report; any laboratory values reported by the authors are in the case record.
resident.physical_exam: Neurologic examination revealed a motor and sensory deficit in the lower limbs with 3 out of 5 muscle strength and loss of sensation to light touch in the bilateral lower extremities up to the level of the upper thighs. The upper extremities showed 4 out of 5 strength bilaterally, with a notable claw hand deformity of the left hand. Sensation to light touch was diminished in the distal upper extremities. Reflexes were not documented.
key_positive_signs: 3/5 motor strength in bilateral lower extremities
Loss of light touch sensation in bilateral lower extremities up to the upper thighs
Claw hand deformity of the left hand
Diminished light touch sensation in distal upper extremities
Extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) along the spinal cord on CT
Severe central canal stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4
Severe bilateral neural foraminal stenosis in cervical and lumbar spine
resident.past_history: Medical history included severe diabetes mellitus complicated by peripheral neuropathy and a foot ulcer, and chronic urinary incontinence treated with a bladder stimulator.
resident.public_message: A 44-year-old female presented with a nine-month history of progressive lower extremity weakness and difficulty walking, along with worsening lower extremity numbness, low back pain, bowel incontinence, neck pain, and upper extremity numbness and weakness. Examination showed 3/5 strength and loss of light touch sensation in bilateral lower extremities up to the upper thighs, 4/5 upper extremity strength, a left claw hand deformity, and diminished distal upper extremity sensation. Reflexes were not documented. CT of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine demonstrated extensive OPLL and severe central canal stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4, plus severe bilateral neural foraminal stenosis in the cervical and lumbar spine. Past history includes severe diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and a foot ulcer, and chronic urinary incontinence treated with a bladder stimulator. No separate laboratory results are documented.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; films were not available for review. The record describes extensive OPLL with prominent osteophytes producing severe central canal stenosis at C3-5, T6-10, and L3-4, with severe bilateral neural foraminal stenosis in the cervical and lumbar spine. T6-10 is the dominant reported thoracic region. Compression direction and cord T2 signal are not stated in the record. The multilevel severe stenosis provides moderate correlation with the reported extremity weakness, sensory symptoms, and gait decline, although the record also notes diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

neurology.localization: The clinical picture suggests a compressive myelopathy, most likely from severe central canal stenosis at C3-5 and T6-10, given progressive lower extremity weakness (3/5) and bowel incontinence. Upper extremity weakness (4/5) and distal sensory loss may arise from cervical cord involvement or radiculopathy, but the left claw hand indicates a lower cervical (C8/T1) root or ulnar nerve lesion, not directly from central stenosis at C3-5. The sensory level to light touch at the upper thighs is lower than expected for T6-10 cord compression and likely reflects superimposed diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Reflexes were not documented, so upper motor neuron signs cannot be confirmed; localization rests on an incomplete examination.

red_flags.finding: Long-standing diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy and foot ulcer
red_flags.rationale: This can cause length-dependent sensory loss and contribute to lower extremity weakness, potentially obscuring a cord sensory level; it does not negate the structural cord compression as a cause of progressive weakness and bowel incontinence, so it coexists rather than changes the indication.

red_flags.finding: Left claw hand deformity and distal upper extremity sensory loss
red_flags.rationale: These findings suggest an ulnar neuropathy or C8/T1 radiculopathy, which is not explained by the central stenosis at C3-5 or T6-10. While it may require further evaluation (e.g., EMG/NCS) and could influence cervical foraminal decompression if radicular, it does not alter the primary indication for treating the compressive myelopathy.

red_flags.finding: Chronic urinary incontinence treated with a bladder stimulator
red_flags.rationale: Pre-existing bladder dysfunction limits the specificity of urinary symptoms as a localizing sign for the current cord compression; however, new bowel incontinence remains supportive of myelopathy. This does not change the need to address the stenosis.

Absence of reflex findings prevents confirmation of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) that would support a myelopathic localization. It does not alter the decision given the severe stenosis but reduces diagnostic certainty.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The sensory level to light touch at the upper thighs corresponds to an L1-2 dermatomal level, which is lower than the expected level from severe T6-10 stenosis; this likely reflects diabetic peripheral neuropathy rather than a true cord level. In addition, the left claw hand is not directly produced by central canal stenosis at C3-5 and suggests a focal ulnar or C8/T1 radicular lesion.
neurology.public_message: Localization: The findings are consistent with multilevel compressive myelopathy, most likely from severe thoracic (T6-10) and/or cervical (C3-5) stenosis, causing progressive lower extremity weakness and bowel dysfunction; however, the examination is incomplete because reflexes were not documented. Coexisting diabetic peripheral neuropathy likely contributes to sensory loss (stocking distribution) and may obscure a cord sensory level. The left claw hand suggests an additional ulnar or C8/T1 radicular process. Red flags: (1) diabetic peripheral neuropathy—coexisting; (2) left claw hand—coexisting (may warrant ulnar nerve/C8-T1 workup but does not change main indication); (3) chronic urinary incontinence with bladder stimulator—coexisting (pre-existing, so urinary symptoms not reliable); (4) absent reflex documentation—coexisting (limits UMN confirmation). Overall match between symptoms and imaging is medium: severe multilevel stenosis explains the dominant syndrome but not every finding.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade: III. Intraoperative MAP target: 70 mmHg. Blood loss risk: high. Extubation difficulty: unassessable due to absence of airway assessment on record. Prone position tolerance: unassessable due to lack of cardiopulmonary assessment.

preconditions_for_failure: Progression of lower extremity weakness (decline of ≥1 MRC grade in any muscle group) despite adherence to therapy
New or worsening bowel or bladder dysfunction (e.g., urinary retention or increasing incontinence episodes)
New or progressive gait deterioration (e.g., loss of ambulation ability or increased falls)
Development of upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski, clonus) if previously absent, indicating myelopathy progression
physiatrist_opening.public_message: Severe multilevel OPLL with cord compression and progressive myelopathy is a serious condition, and I acknowledge that many patients with this degree of stenosis and neurologic deficit ultimately require surgical decompression. However, I propose a structured, time-limited conservative trial of 3-6 months involving intensive physical therapy focused on core and postural stabilization, gait training, pain management, and close neurologic monitoring. Some patients with compressive myelopathy can stabilize or improve with such programs, but the success rate in this severe presentation is modest—I estimate around 25% chance of meaningful functional improvement. The patient's diabetic peripheral neuropathy and pre-existing bladder dysfunction complicate clinical assessment, so we must rely on objective serial examinations. I will accept that conservative management has failed if any of the following occur: objective worsening of lower extremity strength, new or progressive bowel/bladder dysfunction, further gait deterioration, or development of upper motor neuron signs. Until such evidence emerges, I advocate for a trial of conservative care before considering surgery.

physiatrist_final.proposed_duration: 2-4 weeks maximum while awaiting MRI and EMG/NCS results
preconditions_for_failure: Objective worsening of lower extremity strength (decline of ≥1 MRC grade in any muscle group)
New or progressive bowel or bladder dysfunction (compared to documented baseline)
New or progressive gait deterioration or falls
Development of upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski, clonus) if previously absent
persuaded_by: Director's emphasis that the documented 9-month progressive lower extremity weakness to 3/5 strength makes each additional month of delay a risk for irreversible spinal cord injury, which I had underweighted.
physiatrist_final.public_message: The director has persuaded me that the progressive paraparesis to 3/5 over 9 months, in the setting of severe multilevel stenosis, creates a risk of irreversible cord injury that I underestimated. I therefore accept that surgery is warranted if the pending MRI demonstrates cord compression with signal change at T6-10 or C3-5 concordant with the clinical syndrome; if MRI is negative for cord signal change, a very brief supervised conservative trial may still be considered while EMG/NCS clarifies peripheral contributions. My preconditions for failure remain in force: any objective worsening of strength, new or progressive bowel/bladder dysfunction, gait deterioration, or new upper motor neuron signs mandates immediate surgical referral. I will not block surgery while these tests are obtained. I agree with the director's plan for MRI and EMG/NCS.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 44-year-old woman with progressive myelopathy due to multilevel OPLL. Lower extremity predominant symptoms (paraparesis 3/5, sensory level to upper thighs, gait failure, bowel incontinence) most strongly implicate the severe thoracic stenosis at T6-10; the cervical stenosis at C3-5 likely contributes to upper extremity findings but is less likely the primary driver of lower extremity deficits. The pre-existing diabetic neuropathy and bladder stimulator complicate interpretation, but the progressive course and objective weakness indicate active cord compression. In my judgement, surgical decompression is indicated, and a conservative trial as proposed by physiatry is not appropriate given the severity and progression; waiting risks irreversible cord injury.
proposed_options: Surgical decompression of the thoracic spine (T6-10) as the first and primary procedure, likely posterior approach given OPLL, with or without instrumented fusion.

Staged decompression: thoracic first, then reassess for residual cervical myelopathy; if significant upper extremity or residual lower extremity symptoms persist, proceed to cervical decompression at C3-5 later.
Combined single-stage or two-stage decompression of cervical and thoracic stenosis (more extensive, higher risk).
Conservative trial of 3-6 months as proposed by physiatry (I do not favor this option due to progressive myelopathy).
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Staged decompression starting with the thoracic level (T6-10) because the lower extremity symptoms and bowel dysfunction are the most disabling and likely from thoracic cord compression; cervical decompression can follow if needed after reassessment.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for a 3-6 month conservative trial. The patient has progressive myelopathy with 3/5 lower extremity strength and bowel incontinence over 9 months; delaying surgery risks irreversible neurological decline, and the modest chance of improvement with conservative care does not justify that risk.

There is genuine uncertainty about whether to address cervical, thoracic, or both levels concurrently. While I favor thoracic first, the cervical stenosis is also severe and may need staged treatment; we need a plan that prioritizes the most symptomatic level without undertreating.

The imaging is incomplete for surgical planning: CT alone does not show cord signal change or the exact direction of compression; I would want MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine before finalizing the operative plan.

The left claw hand and absent reflexes raise the possibility of additional peripheral nerve or root pathology (e.g., ulnar neuropathy or C8/T1 radiculopathy) that could confound the assessment of cervical myelopathy and should be clarified with EMG/NCS.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that surgical decompression should proceed now rather than a conservative trial, or do you want to explore the conservative option further?
Which levels should be decompressed in the first operation: thoracic alone, cervical alone, or combined? Should we stage and reassess?
Should we obtain additional MRI and EMG/NCS before making the final operative decision, or is the current information sufficient to proceed?
What is your preferred approach to the thoracic OPLL (posterior decompression versus anterior)? I defer the technical approach to your judgement.
vice_opinions.public_message: Based on the progressive paraparesis and bowel incontinence, I favour urgent surgical decompression of the thoracic stenosis (T6-10) as the first stage, with cervical decompression later if needed. I believe conservative management is not appropriate here. However, there are open questions: we need better imaging (MRI) and clarification of the left claw hand. I have laid out options and my reasoning and defer the final decision to the director.

vice_opinions.assessment: I agree with the director that surgery is indicated and should not be delayed by a 3–6 month conservative trial. The patient has progressive myelopathy with 3/5 lower extremity strength, bowel incontinence, and severe multilevel stenosis; the physiatrist's points about confounding neuropathy are valid but the risk of irreversible cord injury outweighs the low chance of meaningful conservative improvement. The main unresolved issue is localizing the primary compression level between T6-10 and C3-5, and excluding a peripheral ulnar neuropathy. I favour urgent MRI and EMG as ordered, followed by staged decompression targeting the level with the greatest concordance between clinical and imaging findings.
proposed_options: Urgent cervical-thoracic MRI and EMG/NCS, then staged surgical decompression starting with the level showing cord signal change or concordant severe stenosis (likely T6-10 first).
If MRI is inconclusive or shows no cord signal change but severe stenosis at T6-10, proceed with thoracic decompression first based on predominant lower extremity myelopathy, then reassess cervical.
Consider simultaneous versus staged decompression if both cervical and thoracic cord compression are severe and clinical picture is mixed.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Proceed urgently to MRI and EMG, then perform thoracic decompression first unless imaging/EMG clearly localizes the primary lesion to the cervical level.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's contention that bowel incontinence may be chronic and not a new red flag deserves objective verification via anal sphincter tone and history; I would not delay surgery on that basis but it may affect urgency.

The relative contribution of lumbar L3-4 stenosis to leg weakness should be addressed: should we include lumbar decompression in the same or later stage if thoracic decompression alone does not explain the deficits?
Whether to proceed with surgery if MRI shows severe stenosis but no T2 cord signal change remains an open question; I lean yes based on clinical progression, but want the director's ruling.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we set a firm timeframe for MRI and EMG (e.g., complete within 48-72 hours) and if so, is the patient admitted for monitoring during that workup?
If MRI shows severe multilevel compression without focal cord signal change, do you agree to proceed with thoracic decompression first based on the leg-dominant myelopathy?
Do you want simultaneous cervical and thoracic decompression considered if both levels appear severe and concordant after workup, or is staged always preferred?
vice_opinions.public_message: My assessment is that surgery is unequivocally indicated; the physiatrist's conservative trial risks irreversible cord injury. I agree with the director's staging plan contingent on MRI and EMG, with a preference for thoracic decompression first if that level shows concordant compression or signal change. I raise three open questions: the reliability of bowel incontinence as a new finding, the contribution of lumbar stenosis, and how to proceed if MRI lacks cord signal change.

director_rulings.public_message:
Thank you all. Before I rule, I want explicit input from several colleagues. Chief Resident, please perform and document a complete neurological examination today—deep tendon reflexes, plantar responses, anal sphincter tone—because the absent reflexes are a gap we can fix immediately. Neurologist, please give your specific opinion: is the lower extremity weakness primarily from the thoracic T6-10 stenosis or the cervical C3-5 stenosis, and should EMG/NCS be done now or after the MRI? Anesthesiologist, please complete a preoperative airway and cardiopulmonary assessment and tell us whether you foresee any issue with prone positioning for a long posterior decompression. Radiologist, please protocol the MRI and tell us what sequences you need to assess cord signal and compression direction.

My current position: surgery is indicated. The progressive paraparesis with 3/5 lower extremity strength and bowel incontinence over 9 months, with severe multilevel stenosis, outweighs the ~25% chance of meaningful improvement with conservative care. I acknowledge Dr. Physiatrist's valid point that chronic diabetic neuropathy and pre-existing bladder dysfunction confuse the picture, and I adopt his proposed failure criteria as part of our monitoring after surgery if we proceed. However, I will not accept a 3-6 month trial when the main risk is irreversible cord injury.

I am not ready to finalize the surgical plan because MRI and EMG/NCS are needed to determine the primary compression level and avoid missing a peripheral ulnar neuropathy. I am ordering MRI cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast and EMG/NCS. I will reconvene with results and with your specific opinions. If the MRI shows cord edema or myelomalacia at T6-10, the first stage will be thoracic decompression; if the cervical cord signal is worse or the EMG shows C8/T1 radiculopathy, we will reconsider whether cervical decompression should come first. We will make that final decision together.

director_rulings.final_decision: We close this meeting to obtain further workup: MRI cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast, EMG/NCS, complete neurological examination including reflexes and sphincter tone, and anesthesia airway/cardiopulmonary evaluation. The patient is to be admitted for close monitoring; all studies to be completed within 72 hours. Surgery is indicated for progressive myelopathy from severe multilevel stenosis, and my tentative plan is staged decompression, thoracic first, but final staging will be decided after results per contingencies: if MRI shows T6-10 cord signal change or concordant compression, thoracic decompression first; if cervical cord signal is worse or EMG shows C8/T1 radiculopathy, cervical decompression first; if both levels are severe and concordant, we will discuss simultaneous vs staged; if MRI shows severe stenosis without T2 signal change, I will still proceed with thoracic decompression first based on leg-dominant myelopathy, as long as clinical progression continues and no peripheral cause on EMG explains the deficit. We reconvene immediately upon results.
delegated_tasks: Chief Resident: perform and document complete neurological examination today including DTRs, plantar responses, anal sphincter tone.
Radiologist: protocol and expedite MRI cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast, specifying sequences for cord signal and compression direction.
Neurologist: interpret EMG/NCS and advise on localization after results; clarify whether leg weakness is primarily thoracic or cervical.
Anesthesiologist: complete airway and cardiopulmonary assessment and report on prone positioning tolerance.
Physiatrist: document baseline motor and bladder function now and monitor for any deterioration during workup; notify team if failure criteria met.
Vice Director: prepare staged surgical options, including simultaneous vs staged decompression, for discussion after results.
